live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient with an uncertain vaccination history presents with a contaminated wound.

What should determine whether tetanus prophylaxis is required?

options.C: Blood group and current antibiotic use
options.D: Whether the wound is painful or bleeding
options.E: Penicillin allergy status and wound site

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Immunisation history and wound type
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Tetanus prevention after injury depends on both the wound characteristics and the individual's vaccination history.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Cholesterol and blood pressure have no bearing on tetanus risk. C. Blood group and antibiotic use do not determine the need for tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin. D. Pain or bleeding does not determine tetanus risk. E. Penicillin allergy and wound site do not determine whether tetanus prophylaxis is required.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Tetanus-prone wounds, such as those contaminated with soil or containing devitalised tissue, need an immediate dose of tetanus vaccine if immunisation is incomplete or uncertain; human tetanus immunoglobulin is added for high-risk wounds and for tetanus-prone wounds when immunisation status is uncertain.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Contaminated wound ↓ Tetanus-prone ↓ Vaccination history uncertain ↓ Need depends on wound risk and immunity ↓ Immunisation history and wound type
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, penicillin allergy and wound site — tempting because antibiotics may be considered, but they do not decide whether tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin is needed.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Tetanus prophylaxis is decided by wound risk plus immunisation status.

live_plab_copy.pearl: Chlamydia is diagnosed by NAAT, with a vulvovaginal swab the preferred sample in women; treatment is usually doxycycline, alongside partner notification.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Fever, petechial rash and shock: meningococcal sepsis, treat immediately.

options.B: To record his partners' blood groups for antenatal screening

Chlamydia partner notification is not a diabetes-screening strategy. E. Fertility assessment is not the immediate purpose of partner notification.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Chlamydia is often asymptomatic, so partner notification finds and treats infected contacts, prevents reinfection of the index patient and reduces complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Chlamydia diagnosed ↓ Partners often asymptomatic ↓ Untreated partners transmit and reinfect ↓ Treat infected partners and reduce transmission
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, routine fertility testing for partners — chlamydia can affect fertility, which tempts, but notification exists to test and treat contacts, not for fertility work-up.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Partner notification exists to treat contacts and break the chain of transmission.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with painful, swollen joints and a new skin rash several days after developing a sore throat. Which diagnosis should be considered?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Migratory inflammatory arthritis following a recent streptococcal throat infection is a classic feature of acute rheumatic fever.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica affects older adults with proximal girdle pain and stiffness, not post-pharyngitis arthritis with rash. B. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain without inflammatory arthritis. D. Gout usually causes an acute monoarthritis in older adults and is not triggered by a sore throat. E. Osteoarthritis is degenerative and not triggered by a recent throat infection.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and causes migratory polyarthritis, carditis and rashes such as erythema marginatum; diagnosis uses the Jones criteria with evidence of recent streptococcal infection.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, acute polyarticular gout — swollen painful joints suggest crystal arthritis, but gout is unusual in a young woman, is not triggered by a sore throat and does not cause a rash.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Arthritis and rash after a sore throat: think acute rheumatic fever.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 39-year-old woman develops watery diarrhoea and abdominal cramps after returning from abroad. She has no fever or blood in the stool and remains well hydrated. What is the most appropriate general advice?

options.A: Start a 7-day course of oral ciprofloxacin
options.B: Maintain oral fluids and monitor symptoms

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Maintain oral fluids and monitor symptoms
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Most uncomplicated traveller's diarrhoea is self-limiting, with hydration being the mainstay of management.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Antibiotics are not routinely needed for mild, afebrile, non-bloody traveller's diarrhoea in a well-hydrated patient. C. Stopping oral intake increases dehydration risk. D. There is no indication for emergency surgery. E. Corticosteroids are not indicated.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Most traveller's diarrhoea is self-limiting; oral rehydration is the mainstay, and antibiotics are reserved for severe, febrile or bloody illness or vulnerable patients.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Watery diarrhoea after travel ↓ No fever or blood ↓ Well hydrated ↓ Uncomplicated and self-limiting ↓ Maintain oral fluids and monitor
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, a 7-day course of ciprofloxacin — antibiotics feel active for travel-related illness, but mild afebrile non-bloody diarrhoea does not need them and they add resistance and side-effect risk.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Uncomplicated traveller's diarrhoea: fluids and observation, not routine antibiotics.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 7-year-old child develops a widespread rash consisting of small, itchy, fluid-filled blisters. Several lesions have already crusted. What is an appropriate infection-control measure?

options.A: Return to school as soon as some lesions crust
options.B: Give the siblings oral aciclovir to prevent them catching it
options.C: Isolate until the fever has settled
options.E: Avoid susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised contacts

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Avoid susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised contacts
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Chickenpox can cause serious complications in susceptible pregnant people and immunocompromised individuals.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. The child remains infectious until all lesions have crusted. B. Routine antiviral prophylaxis is not given to healthy siblings. C. Infectivity continues until all lesions crust, not just until fever settles. D. Shared personal items can facilitate transmission.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Chickenpox is infectious until all lesions have crusted over; keep the child off school until then and away from susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised people, who risk severe disease.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Child with itchy vesicular rash ↓ Lesions at different stages, some crusted ↓ Chickenpox ↓ Serious risk to vulnerable contacts ↓ Avoid susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised contacts
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, return when some lesions crust — crusting does mark the end of infectivity, but only once all lesions have crusted, not just some.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Chickenpox is infectious until every lesion has crusted; protect vulnerable contacts.

options.A: Treat the partner if symptoms develop
options.B: Test the partner in 6 months if still asymptomatic
options.C: Advise abstinence for six months after treatment

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Partner notification, testing and treatment
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Sexual partners should be appropriately notified and tested, and treated where indicated, to reduce reinfection and onward transmission.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Waiting for symptoms risks ongoing transmission. B. Chlamydia is often asymptomatic, so delayed testing risks reinfection and onward transmission. C. Prolonged abstinence is unnecessary; sex is avoided only until treatment is completed. E. Emollients do not treat chlamydia.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In chlamydia, partner notification is essential: current partners should be tested and treated without waiting for their results, and sex avoided until both have completed treatment.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Confirmed chlamydia ↓ Regular partner without symptoms ↓ Chlamydia is often asymptomatic ↓ An untreated partner means reinfection ↓ Partner notification, testing and treatment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, treat the partner if symptoms develop — the partner looks well, but chlamydia is usually silent, so waiting for symptoms allows reinfection and onward spread.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Treat chlamydia partners regardless of symptoms to prevent reinfection.

options.A: A tetanus vaccine booster effectively treats HIV exposure
options.B: PEP should wait until the source patient's result is back
options.C: Seroconversion symptoms typically appear within 24 hours

live_plab_copy.pearl: HIV PEP should start as soon as possible, ideally within hours and no later than 72 hours after exposure; do not wait for source test results when the exposure is significant.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Needlestick with possible HIV exposure ↓ PEP works best when started early ↓ Effectiveness falls with delay ↓ HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is time-sensitive
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, PEP should wait for the source result — it seems to avoid unnecessary drugs, but delay reduces effectiveness; start PEP and stop it if the source tests negative.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Start HIV PEP as early as possible; do not wait for source results.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is admitted with a persistent cough, weight loss and night sweats. What infection-control principle is particularly important?

options.A: Routine contact with other patients on the ward
options.B: Sharing a room with other vulnerable patients
options.C: No precautions until the diagnosis is confirmed
options.E: Turning off the ventilation in the patient's room

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Respiratory isolation and infection control
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB requires appropriate isolation and infection-control measures because transmission can occur through airborne particles.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Unrestricted contact increases transmission risk. B. Vulnerable patients may be at greater risk. C. Precautions may be necessary while diagnosis is being established. E. Appropriate ventilation is an important infection-control measure.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB needs a single room with respiratory precautions until infectivity is assessed; suspected multidrug-resistant TB needs a negative-pressure room.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Persistent cough, weight loss and night sweats ↓ Suspected pulmonary TB ↓ Airborne transmission risk ↓ Protect other patients and staff ↓ Respiratory isolation and infection control
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, no precautions until confirmed — waiting for proof seems proportionate, but confirmation takes time and transmission occurs meanwhile; isolate on suspicion.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Isolate suspected pulmonary TB on suspicion, not confirmation.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient is suspected of having meningococcal meningitis and is rapidly deteriorating. What is the key principle?

options.A: Discharge if the patient remains conscious
options.B: Wait for lumbar puncture results before antibiotics
options.C: Delay antibiotics until a CT head is reported
options.D: Give oral amoxicillin and review next day
options.E: Give antibiotics without waiting for investigations

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Give antibiotics without waiting for investigations
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Suspected bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency and treatment should not be unnecessarily delayed.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Consciousness does not exclude serious meningitis. B. Waiting for lumbar puncture results can cause dangerous treatment delay. C. Imaging should not delay antibiotics in suspected meningococcal disease. D. Oral antibiotics with delayed review are inadequate for suspected meningococcal disease.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In suspected meningococcal disease, give parenteral antibiotics immediately; in primary care, give IM or IV benzylpenicillin before urgent transfer if this does not delay it.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Suspected meningococcal meningitis ↓ Rapid deterioration ↓ Delay increases mortality ↓ Investigations must not hold up treatment ↓ Give antibiotics without waiting for investigations
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, wait for lumbar puncture results — LP helps confirm the diagnosis, but it must never delay antibiotics in suspected meningococcal disease.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Suspected meningococcal disease: give antibiotics immediately; never wait for tests.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient has a deep contaminated wound after stepping on a dirty metal object. What factor is particularly important when assessing the need for tetanus prevention?

options.A: Whether the patient has a penicillin allergy
options.B: Tetanus vaccination history and wound type
options.C: The patient's eye colour and skin complexion
options.D: Whether the patient ate breakfast that morning
options.E: The patient's ABO blood group and rhesus status

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Tetanus vaccination history and wound type

live_plab_copy.pearl: Tetanus-prone wounds include deep, puncture or soil-contaminated wounds; the need for a vaccine booster and human tetanus immunoglobulin depends on wound risk and vaccination history.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, penicillin allergy — it seems relevant to antibiotic cover for dirty wounds, but it does not determine the need for tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Tetanus prophylaxis depends on wound risk and vaccination history.

live_plab_copy.stem: A hospital ward has several patients with diarrhoea caused by *Clostridioides difficile*. Which measure is particularly important for reducing transmission?

options.A: Appropriate hand hygiene and environmental cleaning with suitable sporicidal methods
options.B: Using alcohol hand gel as the only measure in every circumstance
options.C: Allowing unrestricted movement between affected patients and vulnerable patients
options.D: Sharing equipment between affected and unaffected patients without cleaning

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Appropriate hand hygiene and environmental cleaning with suitable sporicidal methods
live_plab_copy.why_correct: *C. difficile* spores can persist in the environment, so appropriate hand hygiene and effective environmental cleaning are important infection-control measures.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Alcohol hand rub is not reliably sporicidal against *C. difficile* spores. C. Unrestricted contact can increase transmission. D. Shared contaminated equipment can facilitate transmission. E. Appropriate infection-control precautions should be maintained.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores; use soap and water handwashing, isolation, gloves and aprons and sporicidal (chlorine-based) cleaning, alongside antibiotic review.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Ward outbreak of C. difficile diarrhoea ↓ The organism forms resistant spores ↓ Spores survive alcohol and persist on surfaces ↓ Appropriate hand hygiene and environmental cleaning with suitable sporicidal methods
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, alcohol gel as the only measure — it is standard ward hand hygiene, but it does not kill C. difficile spores; soap and water and sporicidal cleaning are needed.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: C. difficile: soap and water, not alcohol gel, plus sporicidal cleaning.

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Microscopic colitis is associated with drugs such as PPIs and NSAIDs rather than being the key concern after antibiotics. C. Osteoporosis is unrelated to acute diarrhoea after antibiotics. D. IBS is a chronic functional disorder and is not the serious complication to consider after starting an antibiotic. E. Migraine does not explain persistent diarrhoea.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Diarrhoea during or after antibiotics should prompt stool testing for C. difficile; broad-spectrum agents such as clindamycin, cephalosporins and quinolones carry particular risk.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, collagenous microscopic colitis — causes watery diarrhoea and is drug-associated, but mainly with PPIs and NSAIDs; after antibiotics, C. difficile is the key concern.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Antibiotics followed by diarrhoea: test for C. difficile.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient is suspected of having bacterial meningitis. What principle should guide antibiotic treatment?

options.A: Avoid antibiotics because meningitis is always viral
options.B: Give antibiotics only if the patient develops a rash
options.C: Wait several days for symptoms to resolve
options.D: Treat only after complete neurological recovery
options.E: Do not unnecessarily delay urgent antibiotic treatment

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Do not unnecessarily delay urgent antibiotic treatment
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Suspected bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency requiring prompt treatment.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Bacterial meningitis is a serious and potentially fatal infection. B. A rash is not required before treatment. C. Delay can result in serious harm. D. Waiting for neurological recovery is inappropriate.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Suspected bacterial meningitis is an emergency; do not delay antibiotics while waiting for lumbar puncture or imaging if these cannot be done promptly.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Suspected bacterial meningitis ↓ Can deteriorate within hours ↓ Delay increases death and disability ↓ Do not delay urgent antibiotic treatment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, give antibiotics only if the patient develops a rash — the non-blanching rash is famous, but it is often absent or late; waiting for it is dangerous.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Suspected bacterial meningitis: prompt antibiotics, never wait for a rash.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 36-year-old woman develops a painful, swollen parotid region with fever and difficulty eating. She has not received the MMR vaccine. What infection should be considered?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Painful parotid swelling with fever is characteristic of mumps, particularly in an unvaccinated person.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Scabies causes intense itch and burrows. C. Impetigo causes superficial skin lesions. D. Tetanus causes muscle rigidity and spasms. E. Cellulitis of the leg would not cause parotid swelling.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Mumps causes fever and painful parotid swelling, often bilateral, in unvaccinated people; it is notifiable, and complications include orchitis or oophoritis, meningitis and pancreatitis.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, cellulitis of the leg — fever with painful swelling fits cellulitis in general, but the swelling here is parotid, so a leg infection is irrelevant.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Fever with painful parotid swelling in an unvaccinated person: think mumps.

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Delaying assessment can be dangerous. C. Antihistamines do not treat malaria. D. Influenza cannot safely be assumed. E. Malaria does not require a rash.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Fever in a traveller back from a malaria-endemic area is malaria until excluded; arrange same-day blood films, repeated if negative while suspicion remains.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Recent travel to a malaria-endemic region ↓ Fever ↓ Falciparum malaria can deteriorate rapidly ↓ Exclude malaria urgently
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, assume it is always influenza — flu is common, but assuming it misses malaria, which can kill within days.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Fever after travel to a malaria area: urgent same-day blood films.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 45-year-old man develops jaundice, dark urine and marked fatigue after returning from a region with poor sanitation. What infection is a possible cause?

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Otitis externa causes local ear symptoms. C. Scabies causes pruritus and burrows. D. Tetanus causes neuromuscular symptoms. E. Herpes zoster causes a dermatomal vesicular rash.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Hepatitis A spreads by the faecal-oral route and causes acute hepatitis with jaundice but does not become chronic; vaccination is advised before travel to high-risk areas.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Travel to an area with poor sanitation ↓ Jaundice, dark urine and fatigue ↓ Faecal-oral acute hepatitis ↓ Hepatitis A
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, herpes zoster — a viral illness, but it causes a painful dermatomal vesicular rash, not jaundice and dark urine.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Jaundice after travel to an area with poor sanitation: think hepatitis A.

options.B: Watchful waiting with HIV testing at 12 weeks
options.C: Oral co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for four weeks

live_plab_copy.why_correct: Significant occupational exposure to HIV requires urgent assessment for PEP because treatment is time-sensitive.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Hepatitis B immunoglobulin is for hepatitis B exposure and does not prevent HIV. B. Waiting for follow-up testing misses the time window for effective PEP. C. Co-trimoxazole is used for Pneumocystis prophylaxis, not HIV post-exposure prophylaxis. D. Topical antiseptic does not prevent HIV transmission.
live_plab_copy.pearl: HIV PEP should start as soon as possible after a significant exposure, ideally within hours and not beyond 72 hours; hepatitis B and C risk should also be assessed.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Significant occupational exposure ↓ Source known to have HIV ↓ PEP is time-critical ↓ Assessment for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, watchful waiting with HIV testing at 12 weeks — follow-up testing is part of care, but waiting alone misses the short window in which PEP works.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Significant HIV exposure: assess for PEP immediately, within hours.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Urinary symptoms plus discharge and pelvic pain: think PID, not simple cystitis.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 24-year-old man develops severe abdominal pain and vomiting after returning from a holiday abroad. Several friends who ate the same meal have similar symptoms. What is the most likely explanation?

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Migraine does not explain a cluster of gastrointestinal illness. C. Appendicitis would not typically affect several people who ate the same meal. D. Renal colic is not a foodborne illness. E. Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Several people falling ill after a shared meal indicates foodborne illness; suspected food poisoning is notifiable in England, so inform the local health protection team.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Abdominal pain and vomiting ↓ After a shared meal ↓ Several companions affected at the same time ↓ Food poisoning
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, appendicitis — severe abdominal pain in a young man suggests it, but a cluster of people ill after the same meal points to a shared food source.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: A cluster of gastrointestinal illness after a shared meal means food poisoning: notify.

options.E: To reduce the risk of ovarian cancer in later life

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, reduce cervical cancer risk — STIs and cervical cancer both relate to sexual health, but cervical cancer is caused by high-risk HPV, not PID organisms.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Treat PID early to protect fertility and prevent chronic pain.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Every chlamydia diagnosis needs partner notification, symptoms or not.

Which sexually transmitted infection should be considered?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Chlamydia commonly causes urethritis or cervicitis and may present with dysuria and vaginal or cervical discharge.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Syphilis can cause genital ulceration but does not best explain this presentation. B. Herpes zoster causes a dermatomal vesicular rash. C. BV is not an STI and typically causes malodorous vaginal discharge. D. Tinea corporis is a fungal skin infection.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Chlamydia commonly causes cervicitis or urethritis with dysuria and discharge; diagnose with a NAAT, ideally a vulvovaginal swab, and screen for other STIs.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Dysuria plus discharge after unprotected sex: test for chlamydia.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient is found to have a positive HIV screening test.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Tell the patient immediately that the diagnosis is confirmed
options.C: Arrange confirmatory testing and appropriate specialist follow-up
options.D: Repeat the test years later without informing the patient
options.E: Start treatment without confirming the result

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Arrange confirmatory testing and appropriate specialist follow-up
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A screening test is not necessarily diagnostic. Reactive HIV screening requires appropriate confirmatory testing and specialist care.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. A screening result should not automatically be presented as a confirmed diagnosis. B. The patient's employer has no automatic right to confidential medical information. D. Appropriate follow-up should not be delayed for years. E. Treatment decisions follow appropriate diagnostic assessment.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A reactive HIV screen needs confirmatory testing before a diagnosis is given; explain the result sensitively and arrange prompt specialist HIV care.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Positive HIV screening test ↓ Screening is not diagnostic ↓ False positives occur ↓ Confirm with further testing ↓ Specialist follow-up
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, start treatment without confirming — early treatment matters, but it begins after a confirmed diagnosis and specialist assessment, not on a single screening result.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: A reactive HIV screen needs confirmation and specialist referral before diagnosis.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient asks whether a negative HIV test performed shortly after a possible exposure completely excludes infection.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Explain the window period and the need for repeat testing
options.B: Confirm infection is excluded as fourth-generation tests are sensitive
options.C: Advise that a negative test excludes infection if no symptoms
options.D: Advise repeat testing if seroconversion symptoms develop
options.E: Advise that HIV can be excluded by a negative rapid test

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Explain the window period and the need for repeat testing
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Testing too soon after exposure may not reliably exclude newly acquired infection. Appropriate repeat testing and specialist/sexual-health advice may be needed.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Even fourth-generation tests can miss infection acquired within the window period. C. Absence of symptoms does not make an early negative test conclusive. D. Repeat testing depends on the timing of exposure, not symptoms, as early infection is often asymptomatic. E. A rapid test performed shortly after exposure can be falsely negative.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A negative HIV test taken within the window period cannot exclude recent infection, so repeat testing is arranged once the window period has passed.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Recent possible exposure ↓ Early negative HIV test ↓ Antigen and antibodies may not yet be detectable ↓ Window period ↓ Explain and repeat testing
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, fourth-generation tests are sensitive — they do detect infection earlier, but not immediately; a test taken within the window period can still be falsely negative.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: An HIV test taken within the window period cannot exclude infection; repeat it.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient presents after a significant recent sexual exposure that may have put them at risk of HIV infection.

What is the key time-sensitive consideration?

options.B: Assume transmission is impossible after a single exposure
options.C: Start antibiotics for all sexually transmitted infections without assessment
options.D: Wait several months before seeking medical advice

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Urgent assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis
live_plab_copy.why_correct: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is time-sensitive and should be assessed urgently after a significant exposure.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Transmission risk depends on the circumstances of the exposure. C. Antibiotics do not prevent HIV infection. D. Delaying assessment may make prophylaxis ineffective or unavailable. E. Waiting for symptoms can miss the opportunity for effective prophylaxis.
live_plab_copy.pearl: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis works best started as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours after exposure, via sexual health services or the emergency department.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Significant recent sexual exposure ↓ Risk of HIV ↓ PEP only works if started early ↓ Urgent assessment for PEP
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, wait for symptoms — seroconversion symptoms appear weeks later, long after the 72-hour window in which PEP can still be started.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: After a significant HIV exposure, assess for PEP urgently; time matters.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient asks how to reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections.

Which advice is most appropriate?

options.B: Consistent condom use and appropriate STI testing
options.C: Use two different antibiotics simultaneously for prevention
options.D: Only seek testing if symptoms develop

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Consistent condom use and appropriate STI testing
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Barrier protection and appropriate testing reduce the risk of transmission and help identify asymptomatic infections.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Routine antibiotics after sexual activity are not appropriate prevention for most people. C. Unnecessary antibiotics increase adverse effects and antimicrobial resistance. D. Many STIs can be asymptomatic. E. Some vaccinations reduce the risk of specific infections.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Consistent condom use reduces STI transmission, and regular testing picks up the many infections, such as chlamydia, that cause no symptoms.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Wants to reduce STI risk ↓ Barrier protection reduces transmission ↓ Many STIs are asymptomatic ↓ Condoms plus appropriate testing
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, test only if symptoms develop — it seems sensible, but chlamydia and gonorrhoea are often silent, so symptom-led testing misses infections that are then passed on.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Condoms plus regular testing; do not wait for symptoms.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient is suspected of having C. difficile infection in hospital. Which infection-control measure is particularly important?

options.A: Isolation and handwashing with soap and water
options.B: Alcohol hand gel before and after patient contact
options.D: Airborne isolation in a negative-pressure room
options.E: Standard precautions with alcohol-based hand rub

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Isolation and handwashing with soap and water
live_plab_copy.why_correct: C. difficile spores can persist in the environment, so appropriate isolation, environmental cleaning and soap-and-water hand hygiene are important.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores. C. Bay nursing with standard precautions does not adequately prevent spread. D. Airborne isolation is not the principal precaution. E. Alcohol-based hand rub is ineffective against spores.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Alcohol hand rub does not kill C. difficile spores; use soap and water, isolate in a side room with gloves and aprons, and clean the environment with chlorine-based agents.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Suspected C. difficile ↓ Spore-forming organism ↓ Spores resist alcohol and persist on surfaces ↓ Isolation and soap-and-water handwashing
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, standard precautions with alcohol hand rub — adequate for many organisms, but alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores, and isolation is needed.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: C. difficile: isolate and wash hands with soap and water, not alcohol gel.

live_plab_copy.stem: Which exposure carries a recognised risk of hepatitis B transmission?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Hepatitis B can be transmitted through infected blood and body fluids, including through contaminated needles.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Mosquitoes are not a recognised route of hepatitis B transmission. B. Pollen does not transmit hepatitis B. D. Food is not the usual route for hepatitis B. E. Hepatitis A is classically associated with faecal–oral transmission.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Hepatitis B spreads through blood and body fluids, including shared needles, sexual contact, needlestick injury and mother-to-child transmission; vaccination is highly effective prevention.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Hepatitis B ↓ Blood-borne virus ↓ Spread by blood and body fluids, not food, water or insects ↓ Sharing contaminated needles
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, drinking contaminated water — it tempts as a classic hepatitis route, but water and food spread hepatitis A and E, not hepatitis B.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Hepatitis B is spread by blood and body fluids, including via shared needles.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient is found to have chronic hepatitis B infection. Which organ is primarily affected?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Hepatitis B is a viral infection that primarily affects the liver and can lead to chronic liver disease, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Hepatitis B is not primarily a renal infection. B. It does not primarily affect the thyroid. C. Pancreatitis is not its characteristic target-organ disease. E. The spleen is not the primary site of infection.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Chronic hepatitis B can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, so patients need specialist follow-up and surveillance, and close contacts should be offered vaccination.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Chronic hepatitis B ↓ Hepatotropic virus ↓ Persistent liver inflammation ↓ Risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer ↓ Liver
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, kidney — hepatitis B can cause glomerulonephritis, which tempts, but that is an extrahepatic complication; the liver is the primary target organ.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Hepatitis B primarily affects the liver; watch for cirrhosis and liver cancer.

live_plab_copy.stem: An older adult develops severe pneumonia after staying in a hotel. They also have diarrhoea and confusion. Which infection should be considered?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Legionella can cause severe pneumonia with extrapulmonary features such as diarrhoea and confusion and is associated with contaminated water systems.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms. C. Impetigo is a superficial skin infection. D. Streptococcal pharyngitis primarily affects the throat. E. Tinea corporis is a superficial fungal skin infection.

live_plab_copy.thinking: Recent hotel stay suggests contaminated water ↓ Severe pneumonia ↓ Extrapulmonary diarrhoea and confusion ↓ Legionella infection
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, streptococcal pharyngitis — streptococci are common respiratory pathogens, but pharyngitis affects the throat and does not explain severe pneumonia with diarrhoea.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Severe pneumonia with confusion and diarrhoea after a hotel stay: think Legionella.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Painful testicular swelling during mumps is usually orchitis.

live_plab_copy.stem: A child has confirmed streptococcal pharyngitis. Why is appropriate treatment important in relation to rheumatic fever?

options.A: It reduces the risk of acute rheumatic fever
options.B: It prevents all causes of arthritis
options.C: It guarantees lifelong immunity to all infections
options.E: It eliminates the need for vaccination

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. It reduces the risk of acute rheumatic fever
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Appropriate treatment of group A streptococcal pharyngitis reduces the risk of subsequent acute rheumatic fever.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. It does not prevent all forms of arthritis. C. Treatment does not provide universal immunity. D. Streptococcal treatment does not prevent asthma. E. Vaccination remains important for vaccine-preventable diseases.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Penicillin for group A streptococcal pharyngitis eradicates the organism and reduces the risk of rheumatic fever, so the full course should be completed.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Confirmed streptococcal pharyngitis ↓ Group A streptococcus can trigger rheumatic fever ↓ Eradication lowers that risk ↓ Reduces rheumatic fever risk
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, prevents all causes of arthritis — rheumatic fever does cause arthritis, which tempts, but treatment lowers only rheumatic fever risk, not other forms of arthritis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Treating strep throat reduces the risk of rheumatic fever.

live_plab_copy.stem: A child is diagnosed with scarlet fever. Which general public-health principle is important?

options.A: It is not infectious once the rash has appeared
options.B: It is infectious, so public-health measures should be followed
options.C: Exclusion from school is needed until the rash fades
options.D: All household contacts need routine antibiotic prophylaxis
options.E: It is a viral illness managed with supportive care alone

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. It is infectious, so public-health measures should be followed
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Scarlet fever is a communicable group A streptococcal infection, so appropriate infection-control and public-health measures are important.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Scarlet fever remains infectious until 24 hours after starting antibiotics. C. Children can return to school 24 hours after starting antibiotics; fading of the rash is not the criterion. D. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis for household contacts is not recommended. E. Scarlet fever is caused by group A streptococcus and is treated with antibiotics.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Scarlet fever is a notifiable group A streptococcal infection treated with penicillin V; children can return to school 24 hours after starting antibiotics.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Scarlet fever ↓ Group A streptococcus ↓ Communicable and notifiable ↓ Infectious until treated ↓ Follow public-health measures
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, exclusion until the rash fades — exclusion sounds right, but children can return 24 hours after starting antibiotics; the rash can persist well beyond that.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Scarlet fever is infectious and notifiable: treat, exclude briefly, follow public-health advice.
